questions.stem: After sprinting 200 metres, an athlete continues to breathe heavily for several minutes even though they have stopped running. What is the biological reason for this continued heavy breathing?

options.text: The athlete needs to replace the glucose used during the sprint
Extra oxygen is needed to break down the lactic acid that accumulated during anaerobic respiration
The lungs need time to switch from anaerobic to aerobic respiration
Carbon dioxide is still being produced at the same rate as during the sprint

questions.explanation: During the sprint, anaerobic respiration produced lactic acid. The 'oxygen debt' (also called excess post-exercise oxygen consumption, EPOC) must be repaid — extra oxygen is needed to oxidise the lactic acid, converting it back to glucose in the liver.

questions.stem: A doctor explains to a patient that their blood lactate levels are elevated after a seizure. Using your knowledge of oxygen debt, which process will the body use to deal with this excess lactate?

options.text: Lactate is excreted directly through the kidneys in urine
Lactate is transported to the liver where it is converted back to glucose using oxygen
Lactate is broken down in the muscles into carbon dioxide and water immediately
Lactate is stored permanently in the muscles as glycogen

questions.explanation: Lactic acid is transported via the blood to the liver, where it is converted back to glucose (and then may be stored as glycogen). This process requires oxygen — which is why breathing remains elevated after intense activity to 'repay' the oxygen debt.

questions.stem: Two athletes finish a 400 m race. Athlete X recovers their normal breathing rate in 3 minutes, while Athlete Y takes 7 minutes. What does this suggest about their oxygen debts?

options.text: Athlete X accumulated a larger oxygen debt
Athlete Y accumulated a larger oxygen debt or is less efficient at repaying it
Both athletes have identical oxygen debts but different lung capacities
Athlete Y did not use anaerobic respiration during the race

questions.explanation: A longer recovery time suggests a larger oxygen debt needs to be repaid, or that the athlete's cardiovascular system is less efficient at delivering the extra oxygen needed. Athlete Y likely accumulated more lactic acid or is less fit, requiring longer to remove it.

questions.stem: A student claims that oxygen debt is caused by 'running out of oxygen in the body.' Why is this description inaccurate?

options.text: Because the body always has some oxygen — the debt refers to the extra oxygen needed after exercise to remove lactic acid
Because oxygen debt only occurs during aerobic respiration
Because the body can function indefinitely without oxygen
Because oxygen debt refers to a shortage of carbon dioxide, not oxygen

questions.explanation: The body does not literally 'run out' of oxygen. Oxygen debt (EPOC) refers to the additional oxygen that must be consumed after exercise to metabolise the lactic acid that built up when oxygen supply could not keep pace with demand during intense activity.

questions.stem: During recovery from intense exercise, a person's heart rate remains elevated. How does this help repay the oxygen debt?

options.text: A faster heart rate increases the temperature to break down lactic acid directly
A faster heart rate pumps more oxygenated blood to the liver, where lactic acid is converted to glucose
A faster heart rate prevents more lactic acid from being produced
A faster heart rate forces the muscles to switch to aerobic respiration

questions.explanation: The elevated heart rate continues to pump oxygenated blood around the body. This transports lactic acid from the muscles to the liver more quickly and delivers the oxygen needed for the liver to convert lactic acid back to glucose, repaying the oxygen debt.
